begin-play: Begin Play fires once when this actor is spawned or placed and the play session starts for it. It does not start servers or the match. For example, a patrol arms its one-second timer here, and then the actor is free to stand still.
end-play: End Play runs when the actor is leaving. Use it to stop timers and drop what this actor owned. For example, a pickup uses this to stop its idle sound when the player takes it.
tick: Tick runs every frame. Anything on this line repeats for as long as the actor is alive. For example, writing health here would drain the player while the pause menu is open.
enhanced-input: This is the key or button press. The rest of the function runs only when that action fires. For example, IA_Interact is the use key. The trace does not know which keyboard key was bound.
custom-event: This is a named event. It runs when something else calls that name. For example, a door calls OpenDoor from the interact interface, and that event swings the mesh.
line-trace: A line trace asks the physics scene what the aim hits, and stores that hit. For example, a rifle asks what the crosshair touches, once, when the player fires.
sphere-trace: A sphere trace is a thick sweep. It asks what a ball along the aim would bump. For example, a melee punch sweeps a short ball in front of the pawn and hits a wider target than a rifle line.
break-hit: Break Hit pulls the actor, the point, and the bone out of the trace result. For example, a bullet hole spawns at the hit location, and the bone name picks which limb limps.
apply-damage: Apply Damage tells the hit actor it was hurt, and names the damage type. For example, a rifle that hits a pawn calls this with 25 and a point damage type.
destroy-actor: Destroy removes that actor from the world. For example, a grenade deletes itself after the blast so the mesh does not stay in the level.
play-sound: Play Sound starts a sound at a point in the world. For example, a footstep plays at the pawn's feet when the walk animation notifies.
spawn-niagara: Spawn Niagara starts a particle system at a point in the world. For example, a muzzle flash appears at the barrel when the fire action traces.
set-blackboard: Set Blackboard writes one value the AI can read later. For example, a guard writes the player's location into Target so the behavior tree can chase.
move-to: Move To asks the AI controller to walk toward a point. For example, a patrol walks to the next point after its wait finishes.
activate-ability-tag: This tries to start the ability that carries that gameplay tag. For example, pressing the dash key tries the ability tagged Ability.Dash.
activate-ability-class: This tries to start one ability class on this actor. For example, a medkit tries the heal ability class on the pawn that used it.
apply-effect-self: This applies a gameplay effect to the same actor, such as a buff or a cost. For example, a sprint effect applies a speed buff to the same pawn that pressed the key.
has-gameplay-tag: This asks whether the actor currently has that gameplay tag. For example, a reload refuses to start when the pawn already has State.Reloading.
get-player-character: This gets the character the local player is controlling. For example, a turret aims at the character on player index 0.
get-player-controller: This gets the player controller, the object that owns input for that player. For example, a pause menu asks the controller to show the mouse cursor.
switch-authority: This splits the graph. The authority side is the server. The other side is everyone else. For example, the authority pin subtracts health, and the remote pin only plays the flinch.
has-authority: This asks if this machine is the authority. Shared numbers should change only when the answer is yes. For example, only the listen server should subtract the shared health float.
branch: Branch is an if. One pin runs when the condition is true, the other when it is false. For example, a reload branch stops you when the magazine is already full.
sequence: Sequence runs the following pins in order, one after another. For example, a door plays its sound on the first pin and then starts the swing on the next pin.
forloop: For Loop counts from the first index to the last and runs the body each time. For example, a slot bar walks indexes 0 through 2 and draws one weapon icon each time.
foreach: For Each walks a list and runs the body once per item. For example, a chest walks its item list and spawns one pickup actor per row.
while: While keeps running the body until its condition becomes false. For example, a search keeps stepping along a path until the next cell is blocked.
print-string: Print String writes a message on the screen. It is a trace of what happened, not gameplay. For example, a designer prints the hit actor's name while wiring a trace, then deletes the print.
set-variable: Set stores a value on the component so a later step can read it. For example, Set Magazine adds the rounds that fit. The number stays on the component for the HUD to read.
get-variable: Get reads a value that an earlier Set stored. For example, the ammo HUD reads Magazine so the number matches the last time it was set.
literal: This is a fixed number or name typed on the node. It does not change on its own. For example, a door swing uses 0.4 as the number of seconds the timeline should take.
add: Add sums the two inputs. For example, a scoreboard adds 10 to the old score when a medal arrives.
subtract: Subtract takes the second input off the first. For example, a confirmed hit subtracts 25 from health on the authority.
multiply: Multiply scales one number by the other. For example, mouse look multiplies the axis by a sensitivity of 1.5.
divide: Divide splits the first number by the second. For example, a reload bar divides elapsed time by the reload length to get a fill from 0 to 1.
clamp: Clamp keeps a number inside a lowest and highest value. For example, a limb hit is clamped so a normal shot cannot drop that limb below ten percent.
lerp: Lerp blends from the first value toward the second by the alpha. For example, a camera blend moves from the hip view toward the aim view as alpha goes from 0 to 1.
equal: Equal asks whether the two inputs are the same. For example, a hotbar checks whether the pressed slot is the one already equipped.
greater: Greater asks whether the first number is larger. For example, a jump allows the press only when stamina is above 10.
less: Less asks whether the first number is smaller. For example, a low-health warning shows when health drops under 25.
and: AND is true only when both inputs are true. For example, a vault runs only when the player is airborne and the trace hit a ledge.
or: OR is true when either input is true. For example, a use prompt shows when the trace hit a door or a pickup.
not: NOT flips a yes into a no, or a no into a yes. For example, a sprint stops when the pawn is no longer on the ground.
select: Select picks the first value when the condition is true, and the second when it is false. For example, a crosshair picks red when the trace hit an enemy, and white when it did not.
do-once: Do Once lets the body run a single time, then stays closed. For example, a tutorial hint plays the first time the player opens the inventory, then stays quiet.
gate: Gate holds the exec until something opens it. For example, a cutscene closes the gate so gunfire input does nothing until the scene opens it.
flipflop: FlipFlop alternates. Each call takes the other exit. For example, a light switch turns the bulb on at the first press and off at the next.
delay: Delay waits, then continues. The actor can do other work during the wait. For example, a grenade waits two seconds after the pin is pulled, then applies its damage.
timeline: Timeline plays a curve over time and feeds the alpha out. For example, a door uses a curve to swing from closed to open over half a second.
cast-to: Cast To checks whether the object is that class. The body runs only when the cast succeeds. For example, a trace checks whether the hit actor is a door, and only then asks that door to open.
dispatcher-bind: Bind connects a dispatcher to a function, so that function runs when the dispatcher fires. For example, a health bar binds to OnHealthChanged so it redraws when health is set.
dispatcher-call: Call fires the dispatcher, which runs every function that bound to it. For example, setting health calls OnHealthChanged, and every bound widget hears that call.
make-struct: Make Struct fills in the fields of one struct value. For example, a spawn fills an FVector for the muzzle location before the projectile appears.
break-struct: Break Struct pulls the fields back out of a struct. For example, a hit result splits into a location and a normal so a decal can sit on the wall.
call-function: This calls another function and waits for it to return. For example, the fire action calls Reload when the magazine count is already zero.
interface-call: This calls an interface. The actor that implements the interface does the work. For example, Execute_Interact opens a door or grants a pickup without a cast to each Blueprint.
set-timer: Set Timer schedules a function to run later, instead of every frame. For example, Sense schedules itself every fifth of a second instead of every frame.
set-timer-event: Set Timer by Event schedules an event to run later. For example, a respawn timer calls a custom event two seconds after the pawn dies.
set-timer-function: Set Timer by Function Name schedules a function by its name. For example, a shield recharge names a function that runs three seconds after the last hit.
spawn-actor: Spawn Actor creates a new actor in the world. For example, a gun spawns the projectile at the muzzle when the shot leaves the barrel.
any-damage: Any Damage runs when this actor is hurt. The incoming number is how much. For example, a pawn listens here so a bullet and a blast can both lower the same health.
point-damage: Point Damage runs for a hit at one spot, including where the shot landed. For example, a headshot reads the hit bone from point damage and takes a bigger loss.
begin-overlap: Begin Overlap runs when another actor starts touching this one. For example, walking into a medkit is the overlap. The use key is a different event.
end-overlap: End Overlap runs when the other actor stops touching this one. For example, leaving a safe-room volume lets the threat music come back.
hit: Hit runs when a blocking collision happens. For example, a physics crate plays a thud when another actor bumps its mesh.
on-rep: OnRep runs on the other machines after a replicated property arrives. For example, OnRep_Health plays the flinch after the server's health value arrives.
call-user: This calls a function you added on the component. For example, Interact calls your Open function, and the door graph runs until that function returns.
call-macro: This runs a macro, a reusable chain of nodes. For example, a fire graph calls a recoil macro, and the kick finishes before the next shot can start.
rpc-server: A Server RPC asks the authority to run this. Clients do not apply it themselves. For example, the owning client asks the server to reload, and only the server changes the magazine.
rpc-client: A Client RPC runs on the owning client. For example, the server tells the owning client to draw a hit marker other players never see.
rpc-multicast: A Multicast RPC runs on the server and on the clients. For example, the server tells every machine to play the same explosion effect.
server-rpc: A Server RPC runs on the server because a client asked for it. The owning client cannot change shared numbers by itself. For example, pressing reload on your machine asks the server to fill the magazine.
client-rpc: A Client RPC runs on one client because the server sent it there. Other players do not run it. For example, the server tells your machine to show a hit marker after it confirms the shot.
multicast-rpc: A Multicast RPC runs on the server and on every client. Use it for a shared effect, not for a number only the authority should write. For example, an explosion effect plays on every machine from one multicast.
placeholder: An unknown node is a pasted Unreal node this tool cannot name yet. It holds a place in the chain until you swap in the real node. For example, a custom Blueprint node from another project shows up here until you replace it.
switch-enum: Switch on Enum picks one exit for the value of an enum, or the default exit when nothing matches. It fires when the exec pin into it runs. For example, a stance enum sends the graph to hip, aim, or the default pin.
entry: Entry is the start of a function graph. It fires when something calls that function, not when the actor spawns. For example, Open runs from Entry when Interact calls it.
return: Return ends a function and hands a value back to the caller. The caller's next pin runs after this. For example, a trace function returns the hit actor, and the caller then branches on it.
macro-in: Macro Inputs are the front door of a macro. They fire when another graph calls the macro. For example, a door-swing macro starts here with the door actor the caller passed in.
macro-out: Macro Outputs are the end of a macro. The caller's next pin runs when execution reaches them. For example, the door-swing macro exits here, and the caller then plays the latch sound.
